title: Tenali Raman and the Eternal Flower

full_text:
A foreign ambassador from the Far East arrived at the court of Vijayanagara, presenting an extraordinary gift to King Krishnadevaraya:
An exquisite crimson lotus flower with thirty-two translucent petals, emitting a sweet, delicate fragrance of jasmine and sandalwood.
The ambassador proclaimed:
'Your Majesty! This is the legendary Eternal Lotus of the Eastern Isle!
It never withers, its petals never fade, and its fragrance endures through all four seasons! It is an immortal botanical marvel!'

The King was captivated by the flower's flawless symmetry and scent. He placed it in a crystal vase in the royal diwan, showing it proudly to all visiting kings.

Tenali Raman inspected the flower from a distance.
He noticed that while the palace gardens outside were teeming with honeybees, butterflies, and sunbirds, not a single living insect ever flew near the 'Eternal Lotus' in the crystal vase.

Tenali smiled: 'Maharaj, nature does not create flowers that never wither. Allow me to test this miracle.'

Tenali walked into the palace garden, caught three lively honeybees inside a small glass jar, and brought them into the audience hall.
Tenali stood in the center of the hall, opened the glass jar, and released the three bees!

The bees buzzed into the air.
They circled the hall, flew past the crystal vase, completely ignored the crimson 'Eternal Lotus', and flew straight out the open window toward a bed of common, fading marigolds in the garden courtyard!

Tenali smiled:
'Maharaj, bees are guided by the pure scent of real nectar; they know what is alive and what is dead.
Observe!'

Tenali took the 'Eternal Lotus' from the crystal vase, held it over a small oil lamp, and touched the flame to the edge of a petal.
Immediately, the petal melted into clear, liquid wax with a faint smell of burnt tallow!
The flower was an intricate sculpture made of colored beeswax and chemical perfumes, forged by an artisan to swindle royal honors!

The ambassador hung his head in shame, confessing the fraud.
King Krishnadevaraya embraced Tenali:
'Tenali, thy bees have taught us that artificial flattery and painted wax can never equal the honest, living truth of nature!'
The King rewarded Tenali, learning that true beauty needs no fraudulent claims of immortality.
moral: Artificial imitations can mimic outward beauty, but only living nature possesses the sweet truth of life.

quiz.question: What is the central moral lesson taught in "Tenali and the Scented Flower"?
options: Wit and humor triumph over arrogance and power
Acting in haste and anger without thinking
Believing rumors and flattery without proof
